Rifampin decreases oral contraceptive effectiveness primarily by inducing hepatic CYP450 enzymes, especially CYP3A4, and by reducing estrogen enterohepatic recirculation through alteration of gut flora. Among the choices, decreased enterohepatic circulation of estrogens is the best explanation.
A firm, hyperpigmented papule that dimples inward when squeezed demonstrates the classic “dimple sign” of a dermatofibroma.

The prolonged fever, conjunctivitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, and extremity involvement indicate Kawasaki disease. Its most common serious complication is coronary artery aneurysm due to coronary vasculitis.

Marijuana intoxication commonly causes anxiety/paranoia, slowed thought processing, tachycardia, conjunctival injection, and xerostomia. PCP typically causes severe agitation, hypertension, analgesia, and nystagmus; cocaine causes sympathomimetic toxicity, while alcohol and benzodiazepines cause CNS depression.

The hepatic flexure and adjacent proximal transverse colon are supplied by branches of the superior mesenteric artery, particularly the middle colic/right colic arteries. Sudden ischemia in a patient with atrial fibrillation is most consistent with an embolus occluding a superior mesenteric artery branch.

The standardized mortality ratio (SMR) is calculated as the observed number of deaths in the study population divided by the expected number of deaths based on age- and sex-specific rates in a standard population.

The child has Lesch-Nyhan syndrome due to **hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) deficiency**, an X-linked purine salvage defect. It causes hyperuricemia treated with allopurinol, dystonia/choreoathetosis, and severe self-injurious behavior.

Zinc deficiency causes periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, impaired taste (dysgeusia), and poor wound healing. Her Crohn disease with repeated small-bowel resections predisposes to zinc malabsorption, producing an acquired acrodermatitis enteropathica–like syndrome.

She is Rh(D)-negative with a negative anti-D antibody screen, indicating she is not alloimmunized despite prior sensitizing events. Repeat antibody screening at 28 weeks, administer prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks, and give another dose postpartum if the newborn is Rh(D)-positive.

Chronic *Trypanosoma cruzi* (Chagas) infection causes dilated cardiomyopathy with congestive heart failure (JVD, edema, crackles, S3, orthopnea) and destruction of autonomic enteric neurons, leading to megaesophagus with dysphagia and regurgitation. His origin from Mexico supports this parasitic infection.

The patient has systemic lupus erythematosus, suggested by photosensitive malar rash, arthralgia, fatigue, and fever. Active SLE commonly causes hypocomplementemia due to immune-complex consumption, with increased anti-dsDNA antibodies.

The patient has clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) due to **Clostridium perfringens**, suggested by severe pain, systemic toxicity, crepitus, and gas in soft tissues after trauma. C. perfringens is also a common cause of **food-borne illness** from improperly cooked or reheated meat.

The ECG shows atrial fibrillation, which increases thromboembolic stroke risk. Long-term anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated; it inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing synthesis of vitamin K–dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X.
This patient has an acute dystonic reaction (spasmodic torticollis) due to recent haloperidol use. Acute antipsychotic-induced dystonia is treated with an anticholinergic agent such as benztropine.

Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with paraneoplastic minimal change disease, causing abrupt-onset nephrotic syndrome with generalized edema and heavy proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy.
Ciprofloxacin inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV. Resistance most commonly results from mutations in the genes encoding these enzymes, reducing antibiotic binding.

The patient has delirium tremens due to severe alcohol withdrawal, characterized by autonomic hyperactivity, fever, agitation, confusion, and visual/tactile hallucinations 3–5 days after cessation. Initial treatment is a benzodiazepine such as diazepam to control withdrawal and prevent seizures.

Orlistat inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases, causing fat malabsorption with greasy diarrhea and flatulence. Reduced absorption of fat-soluble vitamin A leads to dry skin and worsening night vision.
Triamterene directly blocks epithelial Na⁺ channels (ENaC) in the cortical collecting tubule, producing a potassium-sparing diuretic effect.
Dog bites can transmit **Capnocytophaga canimorsus**, which causes rapidly progressive, fulminant sepsis in asplenic patients, including those with sickle cell disease.

The patient has relapsing demyelinating disease features, including bilateral UMN signs and worsening paresthesias with heat (Uhthoff phenomenon), consistent with multiple sclerosis. CSF immunofixation typically demonstrates oligoclonal immunoglobulin bands due to intrathecal IgG synthesis.
This is a case-control study because participants are selected based on disease status (interstitial lung disease vs no disease) and prior exposure to the fire retardant is then assessed.

Nortriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant; overdose causes anticholinergic findings, hypotension, and QRS widening from fast sodium-channel blockade. IV sodium bicarbonate provides sodium load and alkalinizes the serum, narrowing the QRS and improving cardiovascular toxicity.

The patient likely has selective IgA deficiency, which can cause anaphylactic reactions to transfused blood products containing IgA due to preformed anti-IgA antibodies. Serum findings show low IgA with normal IgG and IgM.

The patient has cocaine-associated hyperthermia, agitation/immobility, and extensive muscle injury, causing rhabdomyolysis. Tea-colored urine with strongly positive blood but no RBCs indicates myoglobinuria, and serum creatine kinase will be markedly elevated.

The red mass protruding through the vagina with postpartum hemorrhage and shock indicates acute uterine inversion. Immediate manual replacement of the uterus is required, typically by elevating the inverted fundus through the posterior fornix (Johnson maneuver). Oxytocin is given after repositioning to maintain uterine contraction.

The patient has obesity, prediabetes, hepatomegaly, elevated aminotransferases with ALT predominance, and a diffusely hyperechoic liver consistent with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. The underlying cause is insulin resistance, which promotes hepatic steatosis and inflammation. His alcohol intake, acetaminophen use, and autoimmune/viral studies do not explain the findings.

An anterior blow to the tibia causes posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury, producing a positive posterior drawer test. The PCL runs posteriorly from the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibia.

Acute decompensated left-sided heart failure causes pulmonary edema, which increases the alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient through V/Q mismatch and increases diffusion distance due to interstitial/alveolar fluid. The pulmonary surface area remains essentially normal.

Babesiosis causes intraerythrocytic ring and pear-shaped parasites, hemolytic anemia with elevated unconjugated bilirubin, thrombocytopenia, and characteristic tetrad (“Maltese cross”) formations. It is transmitted by Ixodes ticks and can occur in Europe, including the Netherlands.

A left atrial myxoma typically arises from the interatrial septum and can intermittently obstruct the mitral valve, causing positional dyspnea, a diastolic “tumor plop”/murmur, pulmonary congestion, and syncope.

Phenytoin can cause drug-induced lymphadenopathy (“pseudolymphoma”), typically presenting with painless cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy and histologic features that may mimic Hodgkin lymphoma. The recent restart of phenytoin and absence of constitutional symptoms support phenytoin-induced adenopathy.

She has diabetic autonomic neuropathy causing an atonic (hypocontractile) bladder with overflow incontinence: frequent small-volume voids, decreased sensation, and nocturnal leakage. Treatment is bethanechol to stimulate detrusor contraction plus intermittent straight catheterization to ensure complete bladder emptying.

His paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, exertional dyspnea, prior myocardial infarction, and ongoing alcohol use strongly suggest congestive heart failure (possibly ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy). Transthoracic echocardiography is the next step to assess ventricular function, ejection fraction, and structural abnormalities.

The continuous machine-like murmur with bounding pulses in a premature infant indicates a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Pharmacologic closure is achieved with indomethacin, a prostaglandin synthesis inhibitor.

The child has autism spectrum disorder, characterized by impaired social communication, restricted interests, repetitive behaviors, and difficulty with change. ASD is more commonly diagnosed in boys than girls; intellectual disability and impaired attention are not defining features, and onset is typically in early childhood.

The patient has *Clostridioides difficile* infection, characterized by antibiotic-associated watery diarrhea and anaerobic gram-positive rods that form spores. Spores resist alcohol-based agents, chlorhexidine, iodine, and quaternary ammonium compounds; chlorine-based solutions (eg, diluted bleach) effectively eliminate them from surfaces.

The infant has pyruvate kinase deficiency, causing decreased RBC ATP production and chronic hemolytic anemia. Pyruvate kinase is allosterically inhibited by alanine and activated by fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.

The child has symptomatic lead poisoning with a venous blood lead level of 60 mcg/dL and microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling. Levels of 45–69 mcg/dL are treated with oral dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA, succimer). Calcium disodium EDTA and dimercaprol are reserved for severe poisoning (typically ≥70 mcg/dL or encephalopathy).

Chronic prednisone use increases osteoclast activity and decreases osteoblast function, causing osteoporosis and increased risk of fragility fractures, particularly at the femoral neck and vertebral bodies.

A normal A–a gradient indicates hypoxemia due to alveolar hypoventilation rather than V/Q mismatch, diffusion impairment, or shunt. Her obesity and likely sleeping-pill overdose can depress ventilatory drive and cause hypoventilation.

The patient’s withdrawal, poor eye contact, and son’s controlling/frustrated behavior raise concern for elder abuse or coercion. The physician should first speak with the patient privately to assess safety, abuse, and her own concerns before pursuing cognitive or depression testing.

As gastric acid secretion proceeds after a meal, luminal pH falls, stimulating gastric D cells to release somatostatin. Somatostatin inhibits G cells, enterochromaffin-like cells, and parietal cells, contributing to the subsequent decrease in acid secretion and rise in gastric pH.

The thyroid mass shows vascular invasion, characteristic of follicular thyroid carcinoma. Microscopically, follicular carcinoma is diagnosed by invasion through the tumor capsule and/or into blood vessels; capsular invasion is the best choice.

Tumor stage—particularly regional lymph-node involvement and distant metastasis—is the most important determinant of prognosis in breast cancer. Grade, age, comorbidities, and tumor location are less predictive.

Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency due to toxic purine metabolite accumulation, leading to profound T- and B-cell dysfunction, absent thymic shadow, absent germinal centers, failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and recurrent infections.
Menkes disease is caused by an X-linked mutation in **ATP7A**, leading to impaired intestinal copper absorption/transport, growth retardation, and characteristic sparse, kinky, brittle hair.

This patient has complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY), indicated by normal breast development, sparse pubic hair, absent uterus, blind-ending vagina, and inguinal testes. Bilateral gonadectomy is recommended after puberty to prevent testicular malignancy; estrogen therapy may then be provided.

Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation and can irritate the gastric mucosa, increasing the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, making gastritis a contraindication or strong precaution. ECG changes, hypercholesterolemia, tachycardia, and age over 50 are not contraindications.

Rheumatoid arthritis causes chronic inflammation leading to anemia of chronic disease, characterized by decreased serum iron, decreased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and normal or increased ferritin due to iron sequestration.

Diarrhea, vomiting, headache, blurry vision, bradycardia, chronic renal failure, and digoxin use strongly suggest digoxin toxicity, possibly precipitated by volume depletion and reduced renal clearance. The next step is to measure the serum digoxin concentration.

Fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis, right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive sonographic Murphy sign, and mild transaminase elevation indicate acute calculous cholecystitis due to gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct. Normal amylase/lipase argues against pancreatitis, while systemic illness and persistent inflammation distinguish it from biliary colic.

Normal FSH, estradiol, testosterone, and fully developed secondary sexual characteristics indicate functioning ovaries. Primary amenorrhea in this setting most strongly suggests Müllerian agenesis (46,XX), with absent or underdeveloped uterus and upper vagina. POI and Turner syndrome would cause elevated FSH and poor secondary sexual development, while androgen insensitivity causes absent axillary/pubic hair and typically higher testosterone.
The space posterior to the stomach is the lesser sac (omental bursa). It is accessed anteriorly by dividing the gastrohepatic ligament, part of the lesser omentum.

Sudden severe abdominal pain with board-like rigidity, rebound tenderness, and hematemesis in a patient with peptic ulcer disease strongly indicates perforation of a gastric ulcer with generalized peritonitis and likely free intraperitoneal air.

The ECG and irregularly irregular rhythm indicate atrial fibrillation, likely responsible for his recent embolic ischemic stroke. After 1 month with stable infarct and no hemorrhagic transformation, long-term anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated to prevent recurrent cardioembolic CVAs. Heparin bridging is not necessary here.

The researchers selected participants based on outcome status (with or without breast cancer) and retrospectively compared prior exposure to bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. This is a case-control study.

Extending fine striations (spiculated margins) are highly suspicious for primary lung malignancy and would prompt tissue diagnosis and likely surgical removal. Lamellated or popcorn calcification suggests a benign lesion, while a doubling time under 1 month more often indicates infection or inflammation.

The patient has excessive, difficult-to-control worries about health and finances for at least 6 months, along with insomnia, irritability, tension, and impaired concentration. This meets criteria for generalized anxiety disorder.

A membranous ventricular septal defect causes a holosystolic murmur that becomes louder with increased systemic vascular resistance, such as during hand clenching. The other findings correspond to atrial septal defect, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, mitral stenosis, and patent ductus arteriosus.
Dullness to percussion with decreased breath sounds and tactile fremitus indicates a pleural effusion, which most commonly appears as blunting of the costophrenic angle on chest x-ray.

Sudden-onset contralateral loss of pain, temperature, and light touch involving the face and body with preserved strength and reflexes indicates a pure sensory lacunar stroke of the ventral thalamus, involving the VPL/VPM sensory nuclei.

Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding with bruising/petechiae, normal platelet count and PT, and may prolong aPTT due to reduced stabilization of factor VIII. Hemophilia typically causes deep tissue bleeding and hemarthroses rather than petechiae.

This is a volar wrist ganglion cyst producing median-nerve sensory symptoms. The flexor pollicis longus tendon lies within the carpal tunnel adjacent to the median nerve and may become compressed or entrapped by a persistent volar ganglion.

This is a noncommunicating hydrocele, caused by an imbalance between fluid secretion and resorption by the tunica vaginalis. It is a painless, cystic, transilluminating mass with normal testicular tissue and no cough impulse or reducibility.

The patient has acute compartment syndrome with ischemic neurovascular compromise (pain, tense swelling, paresthesia, paralysis, pallor, pulselessness, and compartment pressure 35 mm Hg). Immediate emergent fasciotomy is required to decompress the compartments and restore perfusion; vascular imaging would delay limb-saving treatment.

An unvaccinated child with fever and a pruritic rash beginning on the trunk and spreading to the face and extremities most likely has varicella (chickenpox), characterized by crops of vesicular lesions in various stages of development.

This is a Mallory-Weiss tear, a mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction caused by forceful vomiting. Since there is no active bleeding and the patient is hemodynamically stable, management is conservative with IV fluids, observation, and supportive care.

Chlorhexidine is a cationic bisbiguanide that binds bacterial cell membranes, disrupts membrane integrity, and causes leakage of cellular contents; it is bactericidal at relatively low concentrations. Protein denaturation is mainly due to alcohol, free radicals to hydrogen peroxide, and sulfur/nucleotide attack to iodine.

Tinea cruris (“jock itch”) causes a pruritic, well-demarcated erythematous rash in the groin and perineum with characteristic sparing of the scrotum. It is common in contact athletes such as wrestlers.
Oogonia enter meiosis during fetal development and become primary oocytes, which are arrested in prophase I (dictyotene stage) at birth and remain so until ovulation after puberty.

Hereditary spherocytosis causes chronic hemolysis, increasing folate requirements and leading to folate deficiency with macrocytosis, glossitis, and oral ulcers. Folic acid supplementation would have prevented these symptoms.
Sitagliptin inhibits DPP-4, the enzyme that degrades incretins such as GLP-1 and GIP, thereby increasing glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

Acute worsening of asthma control is most strongly associated with increased airway inflammation, causing mucosal edema, mucus production, and bronchoconstriction. Airway remodeling explains the partial irreversible obstruction from longstanding asthma but is not the primary cause of a recent exacerbation.

The arrow most likely indicates neutrophils filling the alveolar spaces in acute pneumococcal pneumonia. Platelet-activating factor promotes neutrophil adhesion, chemotaxis, and activation during acute inflammation.

The bruising pattern and subconjunctival hemorrhage in a 2-month-old are highly concerning for nonaccidental trauma and are inconsistent with a simple witnessed fall. Suspected child abuse must be reported promptly to child protective services/social services to ensure the infant’s safety; confirmation is not required before reporting.

This is a 2×2 factorial randomized trial evaluating two independent factors—antibiotic choice (nitrofurantoin vs cefpodoxime) and treatment duration (5 vs 7 days)—with participants assigned to one of four combinations.

Iodine deficiency causes chronic TSH stimulation, leading to diffuse thyroid hyperplasia with focal colloid accumulation (multinodular goiter) and hypothyroid symptoms. The enlarged gland can regress after thyroid hormone therapy.

Positive HBsAg with positive IgM anti-HBc and absent anti-HBs indicates an acute hepatitis B infection. IgM anti-HBc distinguishes acute infection from chronic hepatitis B, in which anti-HBc is predominantly IgG.

She has SLE, recurrent thrombosis risk, and a prolonged PTT that fails to correct on mixing, indicating an inhibitor rather than factor deficiency. Lupus anticoagulant antibodies target phospholipid-binding proteins, causing in vitro PTT prolongation but in vivo thrombosis—consistent with antiphospholipid syndrome.

This patient has allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), characterized by asthma, recurrent pulmonary infiltrates/atelectasis, brown mucus plugs, “glove-finger” shadows from bronchial mucus impaction, and markedly elevated IgE. First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone.

Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci occurring singly or in chains are characteristic of **Streptococcus pneumoniae**. Fulminant pneumococcal sepsis with DIC is especially associated with prior splenectomy or functional asplenia after trauma.

This is hereditary angioedema due to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, causing excess bradykinin and episodic, nonpruritic edema triggered by trauma. Intestinal wall edema explains the colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and bowel thickening.
Functional residual capacity is the resting lung volume at the end of a normal expiration, where the inward elastic recoil of the lungs balances the outward recoil of the chest wall.

Severe neonatal hyperammonemia with elevated urinary orotic acid and absent ketosis indicates ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. OTC catalyzes the mitochondrial conversion of ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline.

The mass is most consistent with **struma ovarii**, an ovarian teratoma containing thyroid tissue that can cause hyperthyroidism (weight loss, tachycardia, hyperreflexia, and menstrual irregularity). Teratomas arise from **ovarian germ cells**.

The patient has acute gout (podagra) with needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals. Alcohol use and likely dehydration cause increased organic acid production (especially lactic acid), which competes with urate for renal tubular secretion, producing hyperuricemia and precipitating an attack.

He has latent syphilis of unknown duration, requiring benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 doses. In an asymptomatic patient with a normal neurologic examination, lumbar puncture is not routinely indicated solely because of HIV infection or a high RPR titer. Serologic follow-up should be obtained at approximately 6 months (and subsequently at 12 and 24 months).

Fibrates (eg, gemfibrozil or fenofibrate) markedly lower triglycerides, with modest HDL elevation and LDL reduction. They increase biliary cholesterol excretion, increasing the risk of cholelithiasis.

Maternal hyperphenylalaninemia causes fetal growth restriction, microcephaly, congenital heart defects, neurodevelopmental impairment, miscarriage, and stillbirth. Women with PKU should achieve phenylalanine levels below 6 mg/dL (ideally 2–6 mg/dL) for at least 3 months before conception and maintain control throughout pregnancy.

The patient has ankylosing spondylitis, suggested by inflammatory back pain, heel enthesitis, and elevated ESR/CRP. Extra-articular complications include acute anterior uveitis and aortitis causing aortic regurgitation.

Her episodic chest pain at rest, especially at night, is characteristic of vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina due to transient coronary artery spasm. Long-acting nitrates such as isosorbide dinitrate relieve and prevent vasospasm.

The findings indicate infectious mononucleosis due to EBV. Treatment is supportive, with rest and avoidance of strenuous or contact activities because splenomegaly increases the risk of splenic rupture. Antibiotics and antivirals are not routinely indicated; corticosteroids are reserved for severe complications.

Severe hyperglycemia from poorly controlled diabetes causes glucosuria, producing osmotic diuresis with disproportionate free-water loss. This leads to volume depletion, hypernatremia, high serum osmolality, and relatively concentrated urine (osmolarity 400 mOsm/kg), unlike diabetes insipidus, which causes very dilute urine.

Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR-γ) activation increases insulin sensitivity by promoting adipocyte differentiation and enhancing insulin-responsive glucose uptake. Catecholamines, glucagon, glucocorticoids, and TNF-α promote insulin resistance or increased blood glucose.

Hemoptysis with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and hematuria with RBC casts indicates pulmonary–renal syndrome due to anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies, as seen in Goodpasture syndrome.

He has at least 2 months of anhedonia, insomnia, decreased appetite, fatigue, impaired concentration, and psychomotor slowing, consistent with major depressive disorder. The absence of trauma-related reexperiencing, avoidance, or hyperarousal argues against PTSD; persistent depressive disorder requires symptoms for at least 2 years.

Fluctuating diplopia and fatigable, asymmetric ptosis with normal pupils and intact extraocular movements are characteristic of ocular myasthenia gravis. Pyridostigmine, a longer-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is first-line symptomatic treatment. Edrophonium is primarily used diagnostically, while azathioprine is reserved for refractory or generalized disease.
Warfarin therapy is monitored using the international normalized ratio (INR), which assesses anticoagulant efficacy and adherence and guides dose adjustment to prevent recurrent embolic stroke.
The findings are consistent with Prader-Willi syndrome, which causes hyperphagia and obesity associated with elevated ghrelin. Ghrelin is produced primarily by gastric P/D1 cells.

Lowering the tuberculin skin-test cutoff from 5 mm to 4 mm classifies more individuals as positive, increasing sensitivity but decreasing specificity and positive predictive value. With fewer false negatives, the negative predictive value increases.

The presentation suggests pancreatic adenocarcinoma, likely in the pancreatic head causing obstructive jaundice. CA 19-9 is the tumor marker most commonly elevated in pancreaticobiliary adenocarcinoma.

This is likely benign breast milk jaundice, which presents in a thriving breastfed infant during the first week or two due to increased enterohepatic circulation of unconjugated bilirubin. Breastfeeding should be continued; phototherapy is reserved for bilirubin levels exceeding treatment thresholds.

Leakage triggered by coughing, laughing, and exercise, with urine observed during Valsalva, indicates stress urinary incontinence due to urethral hypermobility from pelvic floor support impairment after childbirth. Normal urinalysis and specific gravity argue against diabetes, primary polydipsia, or lithium-induced polyuria.

The presentation is most consistent with benzodiazepine intoxication causing CNS depression and anterograde amnesia. With stable vital signs and no respiratory compromise, management is supportive care and observation; flumazenil is avoided because it can precipitate seizures, especially in patients with substance use or possible mixed ingestions.

The proximal tubule reabsorbs approximately 65% of filtered sodium, along with water and other solutes. This remains the primary site of sodium reabsorption during volume depletion from vomiting and diarrhea.

Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia beginning shortly after birth with neurologic symptoms suggests Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I, caused by near-complete absence of UDP-glucuronosyltransferase-1A1 activity.

Urea is freely filtered but only partially reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Because water is reabsorbed to a greater extent than urea, the tubular fluid-to-plasma ratio rises above 1, but less steeply than for inulin.

Crohn disease with small bowel resection can cause fatty acid malabsorption. Unabsorbed fatty acids bind intestinal calcium, leaving oxalate free for absorption, causing hyperoxaluria and recurrent calcium oxalate stones (envelope-shaped crystals).
Ichthyosis vulgaris presents in early childhood with fine, diffuse scaling that worsens in winter, spares skin folds, and is associated with follicular hyperkeratosis and hyperlinear palms/soles.

Recent intercourse with a tender, bruised cervix and a closed os indicates traumatic cervical bleeding. Placental location is away from the cervix, and the absence of uterine tenderness or fetal distress argues against placental abruption or vasa previa.

This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), characterized by hyperglycemia, ketonemia, and anion-gap metabolic acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation. Immediate treatment is aggressive IV isotonic fluid resuscitation followed by IV regular insulin; potassium replacement is withheld initially because serum potassium is elevated.

The acute tearing chest pain radiating to the back, hypotension, weak pulses, and tall habitus with joint hypermobility strongly suggest aortic dissection due to Marfan syndrome. Marfan syndrome is associated with myxomatous mitral valve degeneration, producing a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic crescendo murmur at the apex.

These episodes are sleep terrors (night terrors), a parasomnia arising during deep non-REM (N3) sleep, typically in the first third of the night. Children are difficult to console or awaken and have no memory the next morning.

The acute pruritic rash occurring shortly after ceftriaxone is urticaria due to a type I hypersensitivity reaction, caused by IgE-mediated mast cell activation and release of histamine in superficial tissues.

Chronic kidney disease causes phosphate retention and decreased vitamin D activation, leading to hypocalcemia and **secondary hyperparathyroidism**. This produces renal osteodystrophy with weakened bone and predisposition to vertebral compression fractures.

Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, commonly causes dose-dependent peripheral edema due to arteriolar dilation and increased capillary hydrostatic pressure. The other agents are less likely to cause bilateral leg edema.

Elevated bisphosphoglycerate mutase is characteristic of erythrocytes, which lack mitochondria and therefore cannot perform the TCA cycle. Thus, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is absent, while glycolytic enzymes and lactate dehydrogenase are present.

The patient has a prolactinoma causing headaches, visual-field deficits, and galactorrhea. Elevated prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH, reducing gonadotropins and causing anovulation with decreased progesterone production.

Blockade of the interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro) prevents cerebrospinal fluid flow from the affected lateral ventricle into the third ventricle, causing isolated unilateral ventricular dilation.

This infant has late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, occurring at 2–12 weeks in breastfed infants who did not receive neonatal vitamin K prophylaxis. It causes inadequate clotting factor activation, leading to petechiae, bruising, and potentially severe bleeding with lethargy and shock.

The fever, pharyngitis, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, and sandpaper-like blanching rash indicate scarlet fever due to group A Streptococcus. Untreated infection can lead to acute rheumatic fever, which may cause chronic mitral valve regurgitation.

The patient has meningitis symptoms, but CSF findings suggest viral meningitis: modest pleocytosis, near-normal glucose, mildly elevated protein, and normal opening pressure. In the absence of encephalitis features suggesting HSV, treatment is supportive with IV fluids and monitoring.

High-dose inhaled fluticasone predisposes to oropharyngeal candidiasis, presenting with sore mouth and likely removable white plaques without esophageal involvement. Topical nystatin is appropriate initial therapy; fluconazole is generally reserved for refractory or more extensive disease.

The organism is **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**, a non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod associated with catheter-related UTIs. It produces **pyoverdine**, a siderophore that binds iron.

The episodic fever, night sweats, weight loss, cervical/supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and bilateral mediastinal masses suggest classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Reed-Sternberg cells characteristically express CD15 and CD30.
Crown-rump length is the most accurate ultrasound measurement for estimating gestational age during the first trimester, especially up to 14 weeks.

Recurrent nonbilious postprandial vomiting at 3–8 weeks with a palpable epigastric “olive” mass is classic for infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Ultrasound shows an elongated, thickened pylorus.

This presentation is consistent with **trachoma caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis***, common in endemic regions and characterized by chronic follicular conjunctivitis, photophobia, and eyelid swelling. Treatment in children is a **single oral dose of azithromycin**; tetracyclines are avoided in young children because of tooth discoloration.

The t(9;22) translocation creates the BCR-ABL fusion and is a high-risk cytogenetic abnormality in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, strongly associated with poor prognosis. Age 9 is generally favorable, while fever and neutropenia are treatment-related complications rather than primary prognostic factors.

The patient has hematogenous vertebral osteomyelitis, likely due to *Staphylococcus aureus* given IV drug use, fever, leukocytosis, focal spinal tenderness, and MRI/biopsy findings. Initial treatment is prolonged empiric intravenous antibiotics covering MRSA and gram-negative organisms, such as vancomycin plus ciprofloxacin. Surgical debridement is reserved for neurologic compromise, spinal instability, abscess, or failure of medical therapy.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes persistent nonbilious projectile vomiting with a palpable olive-shaped mass and continued hunger. Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid leads to hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

Virologic rebound despite HAART with severe CD4 decline suggests antiretroviral resistance. Resistance most commonly results from mutations in the **pol** gene, which encodes HIV reverse transcriptase and protease—major drug targets.

The patient has symptomatic hypercalcemia (confusion, polyuria, weight loss) with suppressed PTH, suggesting a non–PTH-mediated cause such as malignancy-associated hypercalcemia. Bisphosphonates such as alendronate provide longer-term inhibition of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; calcitonin, IV fluids, and furosemide are primarily acute therapies.

Agoraphobia involves fear or avoidance of multiple situations where escape may be difficult or help unavailable if distressing symptoms occur. It requires symptoms for at least 6 months, does not require panic disorder, and may occur independently of social phobia.
Digoxin increases vagal tone, which slows conduction through the AV node and reduces the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation.
The outbreak produced 500 × 25% = 125 incident hepatitis A cases. The case-fatality rate is deaths among cases: 5 ÷ 125 × 100 = 4%.

The patient has a classic epidural hematoma with a lucid interval followed by rapid neurologic deterioration and ipsilateral fixed, dilated pupil from uncal herniation. In a motorcycle trauma, this is most commonly due to tearing of the middle meningeal artery, producing a biconvex (lentiform) extra-axial hemorrhage.

Nocturnal sweating, tremors, and weakness indicate nighttime hypoglycemia, followed by rebound morning hyperglycemia (Somogyi phenomenon). The optimal intervention is to reduce the daily/evening insulin dose.
Chlorine dioxide is a strong oxidizing disinfectant that damages and denatures microbial proteins, making it effective for sterilizing instruments contaminated with *C. perfringens*.

Poorly controlled maternal type 1 diabetes causes fetal hyperinsulinemia, leading to transient hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (often with septal hypertrophy) in the infant. It usually resolves after birth as insulin levels normalize.

Persistent nocturnal back pain with progressive bilateral leg weakness, sensory loss, and bowel dysfunction indicates spinal cord/cauda equina compression. The hard nodular rectal mass suggests prostate cancer, which commonly metastasizes to the vertebrae and causes spinal metastasis.

The patient has narcolepsy with cataplexy, characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and brief emotion-triggered episodes of muscle weakness. Modafinil is first-line therapy for excessive daytime sleepiness; clomipramine may help cataplexy but is not the best initial treatment here.

She has postdialysis orthostatic hypotension, likely from excessive vasodilation and diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Cooling the dialysate promotes peripheral vasoconstriction and improves hemodynamic stability, reducing intradialytic/postdialysis hypotension and fall risk.

She has serotonin syndrome, characterized by fever, diaphoresis, tachycardia, agitation/shivering, hyperreflexia, increased tone, and clonus. Her stable citalopram dose makes a medication change less likely; adding a tryptophan-containing amino acid supplement increases serotonin synthesis and can precipitate toxicity.

The patient has a pulmonary–renal syndrome with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (hemoptysis, hypoxemia, crackles) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (hematuria, proteinuria, elevated creatinine), most consistent with anti–GBM disease. The presentation is consistent with hereditary spherocytosis causing neonatal hemolytic anemia and jaundice. Spherocytes result from defects in erythrocyte membrane proteins, leading to decreased deformability and increased osmotic fragility with splenic destruction.

This patient has thyroid storm, likely precipitated by infection and discontinuation of methimazole, with fever, severe tachycardia, agitation, diaphoresis, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Propranolol rapidly controls adrenergic symptoms and decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

The patient has Reye syndrome due to aspirin use during a viral illness, causing encephalopathy and hepatic dysfunction. Aspirin inhibits renal prostaglandin synthesis, leading to afferent arteriolar constriction with no significant direct effect on the efferent arteriole.
Atracurium is a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, causing skeletal muscle paralysis.

Phyllodes tumors are fibroepithelial breast tumors that present as rapidly enlarging, large, painless, well-circumscribed or lobulated masses in middle-aged women. Biopsy shows leaflike/papillary projections of hyperplastic, atypical stromal tissue lined by epithelium.

Zenker’s diverticulum is an acquired pharyngoesophageal pouch caused by dysfunction or impaired relaxation of the cricopharyngeus muscle. It commonly presents in older adults with dysphagia, halitosis, and regurgitation of undigested food.

The patient has Guillain-Barré syndrome, characterized by acute flaccid weakness, areflexia, mild sensory symptoms, and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with few cells) after a recent infection. Clomipramine is a tricyclic antidepressant that primarily inhibits reuptake of serotonin and also norepinephrine, increasing their synaptic concentrations. It is particularly effective for obsessive-compulsive disorder.

In a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (Cushing disease), low-dose dexamethasone does not suppress ACTH, while high-dose dexamethasone suppresses ACTH due to partially preserved glucocorticoid feedback sensitivity.

The patient has opioid withdrawal—anxiety, GI upset, mydriasis, diaphoresis, piloerection, tachycardia, and hypertension. Methadone, a long-acting opioid agonist, is used for opioid withdrawal management and maintenance therapy.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome causes proximal muscle weakness that improves with repeated use, diminished reflexes, and autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth. In a heavy smoker with weight loss and cough, it is strongly associated with small-cell lung carcinoma.

Chronic alcohol use can cause sideroblastic anemia, characterized by microcytosis with increased serum iron and ferritin and decreased TIBC. Bone marrow shows ring sideroblasts—erythroblasts containing mitochondrial iron deposits.

Neonatal tetanus from umbilical contamination with *Clostridium tetani* produces tetanospasmin, which blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters—especially glycine (and GABA)—from spinal interneurons, causing rigidity, clenched fists, irritability, and respiratory difficulty.

The patient has osteoarthritis, characterized by activity-related pain, Heberden nodes at the DIP joints, joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation due to progressive degenerative loss of articular cartilage.

Bullous pemphigoid occurs in older adults and causes intensely pruritic, tense bullae due to subepidermal separation. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane.

The clinical presentation and x-ray findings indicate a metatarsal stress fracture. These are managed conservatively with activity restriction/rest, analgesia, and gradual return to activity; additional imaging or fixation is unnecessary.

Bilateral choanal atresia causes neonatal respiratory distress and cyanosis that worsens during feeding and improves with crying because crying permits mouth breathing. A catheter cannot be passed through the nasal cavity into the nasopharynx.

The patient has anaphylactic shock and is treated with epinephrine, which stimulates β1 receptors and increases cAMP in cardiac pacemaker cells. This enhances calcium influx during phase 4, increasing the slope of spontaneous depolarization and heart rate.

This premature infant has signs of intraventricular hemorrhage with increased intracranial pressure (seizures, bulging fontanelle, hypotonia, altered consciousness, and cardiorespiratory instability). Bedside cranial ultrasonography through the anterior fontanelle is the best initial imaging study in a preterm neonate.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes a harsh systolic ejection murmur that increases with reduced preload (Valsalva/forceful expiration against a closed airway), along with exertional dyspnea and syncope. A bifid (“bisferiens”) carotid pulse may also occur due to dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction.

Mumps would cause acute, painful swelling with systemic symptoms, while sialolithiasis typically causes meal-related pain and inflammation.

Masturbation is a normal part of adolescent psychosexual development and does not require testing or treatment when there is no functional impairment, distress, or compulsive behavior. The mother should be reassured and advised to respect his privacy.

The patient has heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), suggested by clinical congestion, left atrial enlargement, hypertension, and an EF of 55%. Sacubitril, a neprilysin inhibitor combined with valsartan, enhances natriuretic peptide activity and provides benefit in heart failure.

Advanced sleep phase disorder causes an abnormally early sleep onset and early morning awakening, with normal restorative sleep. This patient becomes sleepy by 6 PM and feels rested upon awakening, impairing desired evening activities.

Hodgkin lymphoma is classically associated with minimal change disease, causing nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and fatty casts.
This is a Spigelian hernia, which protrudes through the Spigelian fascia along the semilunar line, lateral to the rectus sheath. The rectus abdominis muscle lies directly medial to the hernia.

The erythematous, scaly, tender plaques developing after wearing silver earrings are most consistent with allergic contact dermatitis, typically due to nickel. This is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells and delayed cytokine release.

The findings are classic for ulcerative colitis, which causes continuous inflammation beginning in the rectum with bloody diarrhea, urgency, ulcers, and pseudopolyps. Chronic ulcerative colitis increases the risk of colorectal cancer.

The grape-like vaginal mass, uterine enlargement without fetal parts or heart sounds, and early-onset hypertension indicate a complete hydatidiform mole. It is typically androgenetic with a 46XX karyotype, arising from duplication of a paternal sperm genome in an empty ovum.

The patient likely has familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), suggested by prophylactic total colectomy and annual colonoscopies beginning in childhood due to an affected father. FAP is caused by an APC gene mutation with autosomal dominant inheritance.

A firm nodule attached to the Achilles tendon in an adolescent, especially with premature maternal myocardial infarction, is a tendon xanthoma due to familial hypercholesterolemia, which causes markedly increased LDL cholesterol.

The symptoms, positive anti-transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies, and dermatitis herpetiformis–like rash indicate celiac disease. Small-intestinal biopsy classically shows villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

Avoidant personality disorder is characterized by pervasive social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy, hypersensitivity to criticism, and avoidance of social or occupational activities due to fear of rejection or embarrassment.

Multiple hyperkeratotic exophytic vulvar papules that turn white with acetic acid are condyloma acuminata due to HPV, most commonly types 6 and 11. Prophylactic HPV vaccination helps prevent this condition.

The patient has delayed fever, jaundice, markedly elevated AST, and massive centrilobular hepatic necrosis after exposure to inhalational anesthesia, consistent with idiosyncratic anesthetic-induced hepatitis (classically halothane hepatitis). The patient has fibromyalgia, characterized by chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain, tender points, fatigue, poor sleep, and normal inflammatory studies. Low-dose amitriptyline is effective for improving pain and sleep.

The lung mass is causing superior vena cava obstruction, suggested by facial swelling, headaches, and venous congestion. Impaired cerebral venous drainage can increase intracranial pressure and cause papilledema.
Acute podagra with severe erythema, swelling, and pain in a patient with chronic kidney disease is most consistent with gout, caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in the joint.

Giant cell (temporal) arteritis can involve large vessels, leading to aortic wall inflammation and an increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm.
Frothy, foul-smelling yellow-green discharge with vulvovaginal erythema and elevated vaginal pH is characteristic of *Trichomonas vaginalis*, a flagellated protozoan.

Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is appropriate for comparing mean changes in continuous, approximately normally distributed outcomes across three independent randomized groups.

Fluent, nonsensical speech with impaired comprehension indicates Wernicke aphasia, caused by damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) temporal lobe.

The patient has celiac disease causing malabsorption (bulky, foul-smelling steatorrhea, weight loss, macrocytic anemia) with dermatitis herpetiformis (grouped pruritic papulovesicles). The appropriate treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.

Demeclocycline can cause a **phototoxic reaction**, producing rapid-onset burning erythema and papules on sun-exposed skin. UV light activates the drug, generating reactive metabolites that directly injure skin cells.

The rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, and psychiatric symptoms suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease caused by a prion. Oral candidiasis with recurrent respiratory infections and a history of congenital cardiac surgery suggests DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion), caused by thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia. Hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia is therefore expected.

Diminished ovarian reserve can cause infertility despite regular ovulatory menstrual cycles, particularly with increasing maternal age and reduced response to IVF. The other options typically cause amenorrhea or have supporting histories such as pelvic infection or uterine instrumentation.

Weight gain, exercise intolerance, slowed thinking, and thickened dry skin indicate hypothyroidism. In primary hypothyroidism, decreased thyroid hormone causes compensatory elevation of TSH, making high TSH the most useful diagnostic finding.

A fibroadenoma is a benign, well-circumscribed, rubbery, mobile breast mass composed of proliferating fibrous and glandular tissue. It may become more apparent during pregnancy due to hormonal stimulation.

Bilateral symmetric genu varum (bowlegs) is physiologic in children aged 1–2 years and typically resolves spontaneously by age 2–3 years. With normal growth, development, and gait, reassurance and routine follow-up are appropriate.

The small, firm, yellow, asymptomatic cyst at the cervical os is a nabothian cyst, caused by mucus retention from cervical gland obstruction. These are benign and require no treatment unless symptomatic or atypical.

Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor associated with lipodystrophy, including peripheral fat wasting, central adiposity, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance. The other options are more characteristic of other antiretroviral classes or agents.

The patient has features of multiple myeloma (anemia, back pain, hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency), causing excess monoclonal light chains (Bence Jones proteins) to be filtered into urine. This is **overflow proteinuria**.
Osteopenia is defined by a DEXA T-score between −1.0 and −2.5. A T-score of −1.6 meets this criterion; osteoporosis is ≤ −2.5.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae grows on cystine-tellurite blood agar, producing characteristic black, shiny colonies due to tellurite reduction.

The infant has Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II), characterized by hypotonia, profound muscle weakness, macroglossia, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with heart failure. It results from deficiency of lysosomal acid α-glucosidase (acid maltase).

**Bacteroides fragilis** is an anaerobic gram-negative rod commonly involved in polymicrobial intra-abdominal infections, especially after appendiceal rupture, and is a major cause of postoperative peritonitis and abscess formation.

The patient has psoriasis (erythematous plaques, nail pitting) with inflammatory arthritis involving the distal interphalangeal joints and knee, plus a positive family history—classic for psoriatic arthritis.

Chronic alcohol use with recurrent pancreatitis and steatorrhea suggests chronic pancreatitis complicated by a pancreatic pseudocyst. A pseudocyst lacks an epithelial lining and is instead surrounded by granulation tissue and fibrosis.

This patient has chronic kidney disease likely due to longstanding hypertensive nephrosclerosis. The patient has cystic fibrosis, suggested by failure to thrive, malodorous steatorrhea, recurrent pulmonary infection with Pseudomonas, and elevated sweat chloride. The underlying defect is an abnormal CFTR protein, causing impaired chloride secretion and dehydrated, viscous secretions.

This patient has social anxiety disorder with marked fear of negative evaluation, avoidance, and panic-like autonomic symptoms in social situations. The findings are most consistent with a hemodynamically significant ventricular septal defect, classically a membranous VSD causing a harsh pansystolic murmur and exertional intolerance. The membranous interventricular septum develops from the endocardial cushion.

Eosinophilic esophagitis causes intermittent dysphagia to solid foods and food impaction in young men, often with atopic conditions such as asthma and eczema. It can also cause reflux-like symptoms that are unresponsive to proton-pump inhibitors.

The patient has severe hyperthermia, altered mental status, tachycardia, and recent intense physical exertion at a construction site, consistent with exertional heat stroke. The patient has megaloblastic anemia with leukopenia, glossitis, low reticulocytes, and symmetric peripheral neuropathy with cognitive changes, consistent with vitamin B12 deficiency. The patient has chronic hepatitis C infection (positive HCV IgG and detectable RNA). Treatment should use direct-acting antivirals, such as sofosbuvir plus simeprevir. Interferon or ribavirin alone is inadequate, and lamivudine is used for hepatitis B.

Painless, rapidly developing thyroid enlargement with transient hyperthyroid symptoms and a normal ESR favors silent (painless) thyroiditis. De Quervain thyroiditis is typically painful with elevated ESR, while Graves disease usually causes a diffuse goiter with additional hyperadrenergic findings.

The patient has inflammatory polyarthritis suggestive of early rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and can help confirm the diagnosis, even early in the disease course.

Longstanding rheumatoid arthritis causes chronic inflammation with increased serum amyloid A production, leading to secondary (AA) amyloid deposition in the kidneys and nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and edema).

The neurologic and psychiatric symptoms with dysarthria, dystonia, ataxia, and Kayser-Fleischer rings indicate Wilson disease, caused by impaired copper excretion due to ATP7B dysfunction, leading to copper accumulation in tissues.

The grayish-white pharyngeal pseudomembrane, cervical lymphadenopathy (“bull neck”), and palatal paresis indicate diphtheria caused by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*. Its exotoxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, inhibiting protein synthesis.

Delayed, bilateral upper-extremity weakness and sensory loss with preserved lower-extremity strength suggests a central cervical spinal cord lesion. The patient has hirsutism, acne, and oligomenorrhea with mildly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, consistent with nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Reduced cortisol synthesis causes increased ACTH stimulation and hyperplasia of the adrenal cortex, with excess androgen production.

The skip lesions involving the terminal ileum and transverse colon, systemic inflammation, and negative infectious studies suggest Crohn disease. Noncaseating granulomas on biopsy are the most specific histologic finding.

The patient has polycystic ovary syndrome causing chronic anovulation, evidenced by oligomenorrhea, obesity, acne, hirsutism, and infertility. After lifestyle modification, ovulation induction with clomiphene is appropriate to achieve pregnancy.

This diabetic man has an atypical acute coronary syndrome presentation (nausea, dyspnea, diaphoresis, and lightheadedness without chest pain). The ECG is most consistent with an acute inferior myocardial infarction, which can also cause vagal symptoms and conduction abnormalities.
